title: Devil's Advocate or Real Dissent
text:
For decades, groups have been advised to fight groupthink by appointing a devil's advocate, someone told to argue against the prevailing view. Charlan Nemeth of the University of California, Berkeley, had spent years studying the creative effects of minority dissent, and she suspected that playacted disagreement was not the same as the real thing.

With Keith Brown and John Rogers, she ran an experiment in which small groups discussed a problem and had to reach a decision. Some groups included a member who genuinely disagreed with the majority view. Others included a member who argued the same opposing position but was openly playing devil's advocate.

Genuine dissent produced more and better thinking. Groups with an authentic dissenter generated more original ideas and considered a wider range of solutions. When the dissent was framed as a role, the majority often treated it as a game. Instead of reconsidering, they tended to come up with more reasons for their original view, so the devil's advocate sometimes ended up strengthening the very position it was meant to test.
lesson: Assigned critics are easy to dismiss. Seek out people who truly disagree with you and give them room to say so.
people: Charlan Nemeth, Keith Brown, John Rogers
source: Nemeth, C., Brown, K., and Rogers, J. (2001). Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent: Stimulating quantity and quality. European Journal of Social Psychology, 31(6), 707-720.
